blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is particularly well suited to code generation because generated programs can be objectively evaluated through execution. Execution also provides behavioral information that can be reused as additional supervision. The Synergistic Policy and Reward Co-Evolving Framework (SPARK), originally proposed for reasoning tasks, exploits this idea by recycling training rollouts and their evaluation results to train a model not only to generate solutions but also to evaluate and improve them. We investigate whether this policy-reward co-evolution approach transfers effectively to code generation and whether execution-grounded reflection provides an additional source of self-improvement. We compare SPARK-style rollout recycling with execution-only Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct. Our results do not support either hypothesis under the configuration tested. Although co-evolution improves training performance, these gains do not generalize to held-out problems. Compared at the same stage of training, rollout recycling produces roughly 34x greater KL divergence from the reference policy than execution-only GRPO. Over training, trained tokens per GRPO sequence fall from 185 to 86 as training pass rate increases, while held-out performance declines or fails to sustain early gains. We characterize these patterns as single-adapter policy drift: the shared trainable parameters increasingly depart from pretrained code-generation behavior without corresponding gains in generalization. The results show that higher training reward alone is not evidence of generalizable code self-improvement and highlight the importance of held-out evaluation and drift diagnostics.

blocks.en: I Introduction
blocks.zh: 一. 导言

blocks.en:
Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable of code
generation, but functional correctness remains challenging. A generated program
may be syntactically valid yet fail edge cases, implement an incorrect
algorithm, or crash at runtime. Because generated programs can be objectively
evaluated through execution, code generation provides a natural setting for
reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), unlike many
natural-language tasks that require subjective judgments of response quality.
Moreover, execution provides information about program behavior that can serve
as additional supervision.

blocks.en:
This work investigates whether such information can be exploited through
policy–reward co-evolution. We build on the Synergistic Policy and Reward Co-Evolving Framework (SPARK) [ 1 ] , a self-improvement
framework originally developed for reasoning tasks. In conventional RLVR,
model-generated solutions, or rollouts, are used to compute rewards and update
the policy, but are not typically reused for further training. SPARK instead
recycles these rollouts and their evaluation results to train the model to
evaluate and improve its own outputs. These capabilities co-evolve with the
policy within a single model. We investigate whether this approach transfers
effectively to code generation.

blocks.en:
We test two hypotheses. First, we hypothesize that SPARK-style co-evolution can
improve code generation beyond an execution-only RLVR baseline based on Group
Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [ 2 ] , including its ability
to generalize to problems not seen during training. Second, we hypothesize that
execution-grounded reflection, in which the model learns to revise failing code
using unit-test feedback, can provide an additional source of self-improvement.

We evaluate these hypotheses using the Mostly Basic Python Problems
(MBPP) [ 3 ] and HumanEval [ 4 ] datasets. We train on a
subset of MBPP and evaluate generalization both on held-out MBPP problems and
on HumanEval as a separate, fully held-out benchmark. This design allows us
to distinguish improvements on the training problems from in-distribution
generalization within MBPP and cross-benchmark generalization to HumanEval.

blocks.en:
Our experiments do not support either hypothesis under the configuration
tested. Although co-evolution improves performance on the training problems,
these gains do not generalize to unseen problems. At the same time, the model
increasingly departs from its pretrained behavior, as measured by KL
divergence. The model also produces progressively shorter outputs during
training. We characterize these patterns as single-adapter policy drift,
arising when the same trainable parameters are used both to generate code and
to learn to evaluate it.

blocks.en:
This paper makes three contributions. First, we adapt SPARK-style
policy–reward co-evolution to code generation by using information from
program execution as additional supervision. Second, we evaluate whether this
approach improves code-generation performance and generalization beyond
execution-only GRPO. Third, we analyze policy drift to examine the relationship
between training improvement and held-out generalization. Our findings
highlight limitations of the single-adapter co-evolution design studied here
and motivate further investigation of alternative designs for code generation.

blocks.en: II Background
blocks.zh: 二. 背景情况

blocks.en: II-A RLVR and GRPO
blocks.zh: 二-A RLVR和GRPO

blocks.en:
Code-generation LLMs are typically built through large-scale pretraining on
code corpora [ 5 , 6 ] followed by instruction tuning and
reinforcement learning from human feedback, which optimizes the model against a
reward model learned from human preferences [ 7 ] . RLVR
replaces that learned reward model with an executable or rule-based verifier.
DeepSeekMath introduced GRPO in this setting, and DeepSeek-R1 showed that RLVR
can produce strong reasoning behavior [ 2 , 8 ] . Related
work also improves models at inference time rather than training time, for
example by spending more computation on difficult problems [ 9 ] .

blocks.en: II-B Self-Correction and SCoRe
blocks.zh: II-B 自更正和SCoRE

blocks.en:
In this paper, reflection means training the model to repair its own
failing code: given a program that failed its unit tests and the resulting
error message, the model learns to produce a corrected program.
Self-Correction via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe) [ 10 ] motivates this
part of our work. SCoRe trains a model in a multi-turn setting: the
model first produces an initial answer and then, conditioned on its own first
answer, produces a revised answer. SCoRe identifies two failure modes directly
relevant to execution-grounded code repair: distribution shift , when
correction examples do not match the model’s own current mistakes, and behavior collapse , when the model learns conservative or minimal edits
instead of meaningful repairs. These ideas help interpret our reflection
results: although we use execution traces and on-policy rollouts, reflection is
still trained as auxiliary supervised fine-tuning (SFT) rather than as a
dedicated multi-turn repair objective optimized with reinforcement learning.

blocks.en: II-C SPARK-Style Rollout Recycling
blocks.zh: II-C SPARK-Style推出回收

blocks.en:
For each generated program, execution provides correctness, the fraction of
tests passed, the error type, and the error message. SPARK [ 1 ] turns
these into three auxiliary objectives for the same model: pointwise judgment (predict whether a candidate is correct), pairwise comparison (choose the better of two candidates), and reflection (repair failing code). Related approaches that train a
policy together with its own reward signal include Cooper [ 11 ] ,
CURE [ 12 ] , and self-rewarding language models [ 13 ] .

blocks.en:
In our implementation, pointwise judgment is not used (weight 0.00), because
its one-word targets such as “Correct” or “Incorrect” differ sharply from
the full programs the same model must generate. For pairwise comparison, each
failing rollout of a problem is paired with a randomly chosen passing rollout
of the same problem, with the order in which the two are shown randomized.
Reflection is the dominant auxiliary objective, since learning to repair code
from execution feedback is the main adaptation from reasoning tasks to code.
For reflection, the model is shown its failing program and the error message,
and is trained to output a correct program for the same problem: a passing
rollout from the same batch when one exists, and otherwise the canonical solution provided with MBPP.

blocks.en: II-D Policy Drift as a Central Risk
blocks.zh: II-D 政策流动作为一种中心风险

blocks.en:
We fine-tune with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 14 ] , which trains a small
set of added weights, an adapter , while the pretrained model stays
frozen. A central risk in co-evolutionary training is that the auxiliary
objectives update the same adapter used for code generation. Their targets look
very different from ordinary code completions: a pairwise answer is a single
token, and a reflection target is a program written in response to a different
prompt. Training on this mixture can shift the adapter away from how the
pretrained model writes code. Such a shift can raise training reward without
improving, and possibly while harming, performance on unseen problems. We
track two signals of this drift. The first is the KL divergence between the
trained model and the frozen pretrained model, which measures how far its
output distribution has moved. The second is the trained tokens per GRPO sequence: the average length, in
generated tokens, of the solutions used in each GRPO update. Shorter outputs
are not harmful in themselves, but a sharp drop suggests the adapter is being
pulled toward the short auxiliary targets.
Following SPARK [ 1 ] , we also add the KL divergence to the training
loss as a penalty; if KL still grows substantially, the penalty is not
preventing drift.

blocks.en: III Methodology
blocks.zh: 三、结 论 方法

blocks.en: III-A Model and Fine-Tuning Setup
blocks.zh: III-A 模式和精致设置

blocks.en:
All experiments fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-3B-Instruct with QLoRA [ 15 ] ,
which loads the pretrained weights in compressed 4-bit form and keeps them
frozen, so that only the LoRA adapter is trained. Following the QLoRA
recommendation, the adapter is applied to all attention and feed-forward
projection layers, giving 29.9M trainable parameters out of 3.1B (about
0.96%). We chose the 3B model so that repeated rounds of generation,
execution, and training fit within our available hardware.

blocks.en: III-B Training Objective
blocks.zh: 三-B 培训目标

blocks.en:
Each training iteration of the co-evolution condition updates the same adapter
in two phases. The first is a standard GRPO update [ 2 ] , which
increases the probability of solutions with positive advantage
in ( 1 ) and decreases it for those with negative advantage.
Each update is clipped so the model cannot change too much in a single step,
and the KL penalty with weight β \beta discourages drift from the frozen
pretrained model. The second phase is auxiliary supervised fine-tuning on the
recycled rollouts, minimizing ℒ aux ​ ( θ ) = λ aux ​ ( w pair ​ ℒ pair ​ ( θ ) + w refl ​ ℒ refl ​ ( θ ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}(\theta)=\lambda_{\mathrm{aux}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{pair}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}(\theta)+w_{\mathrm{refl}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{refl}}(\theta)\bigr), (2) where θ \theta are the adapter parameters, ℒ pair \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}} and ℒ refl \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{refl}} are the standard next-token prediction losses on
the pairwise and reflection targets, computed on the target response only and
not on the prompt, and w pair w_{\mathrm{pair}} and w refl w_{\mathrm{refl}} are the weights in Table I . The
overall scale λ aux \lambda_{\mathrm{aux}} controls how strongly the auxiliary
phase moves the adapter relative to the GRPO phase, since both share one
optimizer. The execution-only baseline runs the GRPO phase alone; the
co-evolution condition runs both, so both update the same shared adapter,
which is the design choice under test. The values of β \beta and λ aux \lambda_{\mathrm{aux}} for each configuration are given in
Section IV .

blocks.en: III-C Datasets, Execution, and Reward
blocks.zh: 三-C 数据集、执行和奖励

blocks.en:
We use the MBPP-sanitized subset [ 3 ] , a hand-verified version of MBPP
curated by its original authors to remove ambiguous task descriptions, poorly
specified requirements, and broken test assertions. We keep the 411 problems
whose unit tests can be parsed automatically and randomly split them, with a
fixed seed, into 311 training and 100 held-out problems.
HumanEval [ 4 ] (164 problems) serves as a second, fully held-out
benchmark.
blocks.zh:
我们使用 MBPP 化的子集 [3], MBPP 的手验证版本
由原作者编写,删除模糊的任务说明,但内容差
具体要求,以及破解的测试断言。 我们保留411个问题
其单位测试可自动和随机地进行分解,并带有
固定种子 311个训练 和100个被搁置的问题

基准。

blocks.en:
To score a solution, we extract the Python code from the model’s response and
run it with the problem’s unit tests in a separate, isolated process. Each run
is limited to 10 seconds and 2 GB of memory, enough for even naive brute-force
solutions on these small problems while stopping infinite loops and runaway
memory use. During training, each unit test is run separately, and a
solution’s reward is the proportion of its unit tests that pass, reduced by a
penalty if the code has a syntax error, raises a runtime error, or times out.

为了得到一个解决方案,我们从模型的反应中提取Python代码,
在一个单独、孤立的进程中用问题的单元测试来运行它。 每次运行
仅限10秒2GB的内存 足够天真野蛮的力量了
解决这些小问题,同时停止无限循环和逃跑
内存使用. 在培训期间,每个单元的测试分开进行,a
解决方案的奖励是其单位测试通过的比例,减去
如果代码有语法错误,则会引发运行时间错误,或出错。

blocks.en:
These rewards are the r i r_{i} in ( 1 ), computed for the K K candidate solutions in each GRPO group. We start with K = 4 K=4 solutions per
problem. If all of them receive the same reward, the group carries no learning
signal, so we sample more, up to K = 8 K=8 , until the rewards differ or the cap is
reached.

问题。 如果所有人都得到同样的奖赏, 团体没有学习

blocks.zh: III-D 实验设计

the same shared adapter. Condition A therefore measures what execution-only

evaluate several settings of Condition C that differ in how strongly the

blocks.en: III-E Evaluation Metrics
blocks.zh: 三-E 评价计量

blocks.en:
We evaluate each checkpoint on two held-out sets. The 100 held-out MBPP
problems measure generalization to unseen problems from the benchmark used in
training. HumanEval, which is never used in training, measures whether training
generalizes to entirely unseen data from a separate benchmark. For each
problem, we generate five solutions at temperature 0.2 and report pass@1 and
pass@5, where pass@ k k is the probability that at least one of k k solutions
passes all tests; pass@1 is thus the average fraction of the five that pass,
and pass@5 whether any of them does. HumanEval pass@1 is our primary metric,
since it measures single-attempt quality on fully unseen problems. We also
track training pass rate and mean reward (progress on the training problems),
KL divergence (policy drift), trained tokens per GRPO sequence (length drift),
and reflection fix rate (repair ability). Because all experiments use a single
seed and HumanEval has 164 problems, we do not claim statistical significance
for small pass@ k k differences and interpret them together with the drift
diagnostics.

因为它能衡量 完全隐蔽的问题的单一能力 我们也

种子和HumanEval有164个问题, 我们不声称统计意义
用于小过错@ kk 差异并结合漂移来解释
诊断。

blocks.en: IV Results and Analysis
blocks.zh: 四. 结果和分析

blocks.en: IV-A Preliminary Hyperparameter Study
blocks.zh: 初步超参数 学习

blocks.en:
To choose the auxiliary loss scale and KL coefficient affordably, we first ran
a shorter preliminary study: three iterations on 200 of the 311 training
problems, evaluated on the same held-out MBPP problems and on HumanEval. The study compared Condition A, execution-only GRPO with no auxiliary phase, against two
co-evolution configurations: naive (C-light, β = 0.01 \beta=0.01 , λ aux = 0.10 \lambda_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.10 ) and regularized (C-reg, β = 0.02 \beta=0.02 , λ aux = 0.03 \lambda_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.03 ).
Table II summarizes the results.

Three patterns emerge. Execution-only GRPO scores highest on HumanEval pass@1, narrowly ahead of C-reg. Naive co-evolution (C-light) improves MBPP held-out pass@1 and training
pass rate but degrades HumanEval, showing the characteristic divergence pattern
where HumanEval falls and KL grows.
The C-reg configuration, with a lower auxiliary loss scale
( λ aux = 0.03 \lambda_{\mathrm{aux}}=0.03 ) and a stronger KL penalty ( β = 0.02 \beta=0.02 ),
recovers performance on HumanEval to close to baseline and achieves the best
MBPP pass@5.

blocks.en:
These results motivate the more conservative configuration used in the main experiment of the next section, which we call C-reg2: λ aux \lambda_{\mathrm{aux}} lowered from 0.03 to 0.02, the
pairwise weight from 0.1 to 0.05, and β \beta raised from 0.02 to 0.03. The two
changes work together: a smaller λ aux \lambda_{\mathrm{aux}} weakens how strongly
auxiliary SFT pulls the shared adapter, while a larger β \beta restrains drift
from the frozen pretrained model.

the results.

To avoid a misleading best-vs-final comparison, we also compare the runs at

Two factors limit how much weight we place on the pass@ k k comparisons. First, HumanEval contains 164 problems and our experiments use a single random seed, so a

these reasons we treat the KL divergence and trained-token-length diagnostics, both of which

signals, and treat pass@ k k gaps as supporting evidence rather than the central
finding.

blocks.en:
This large drift is consistent with the HumanEval regression: even though only
0.96% of parameters are trainable through LoRA, the auxiliary objective is
strong enough to move the model far from its pretrained behavior. The pattern
also matches recent studies of reinforcement learning for code. For example, a study of self-improving code agents [ 16 ] found that in 73.8% of
GPU-kernel optimization trajectories and 46.8% of algorithmic-optimization
trajectories, the agent’s reward improved without corresponding improvement on
held-out evaluation, with the gap widening as optimization continued; similar
over-optimization appears in code-repair self-play [ 17 ] . We
observe the same widening pattern in our training regime.

blocks.en:
We identify four failure signatures consistent with the observed divergence.
The first three concern the shared-adapter design itself.
(1) Auxiliary target heterogeneity : pairwise outputs (single-token
A/B) and reflection outputs (full programs) differ in length and structure from
normal code completions, so when the same adapter is updated by all loss
signals it is pulled toward a compromise distribution that fits none of the
objectives well. (2) Length collapse : trained tokens per sequence fall
from 185 to 86, consistent with the adapter shifting toward the shorter auxiliary targets.
(3) Single-adapter entanglement : because policy and auxiliary
objectives share the same LoRA weights, the training pressure from each cannot
be balanced through architectural separation alone, even with reduced auxiliary
loss scale and increased KL regularization. The fourth reflects how we
constructed reflection targets, as discussed in the next section.
(4) Weak reflection supervision : the trained
reflection fix rate remains below the pretrained baseline at every iteration.
The baseline repairs 4 of 34 failing programs (0.1176); C-reg2-long falls to
2/33 at iteration 1 and recovers only to 3/36 (0.0833) by iteration 6. These
counts are small enough that we read the metric as directionally consistent
with the other diagnostics rather than as an independent result.

blocks.en:
The progression across configurations (C-light → \rightarrow C-reg → \rightarrow C-reg2) strengthens this reading. Naive C-light caused immediate
HumanEval degradation and large KL growth; C-reg reduced the damage and
improved MBPP pass@5; and the more conservative C-reg2 still drifted under more
data and longer training. All three showed drift away from the pretrained
distribution. In the preliminary study, C-light, with a stronger auxiliary loss and a weaker KL penalty than C-reg, drifted far more; C-reg2 still drifted
substantially despite the weakest auxiliary loss of the three, though it was
also trained longer and on more data. This consistency across regularization regimes suggests the divergence is
intrinsic to single-adapter co-evolution under these objectives, not an
artifact of a single poorly chosen configuration.

blocks.en: V Discussion and Conclusion
blocks.zh: 五. 讨论和结论

blocks.en:
SPARK-style co-evolution is applicable to code generation, but it does not outperform execution-only GRPO on cross-benchmark HumanEval. At the matched
iteration 5, C-reg2 trails A-long on HumanEval pass@1 (0.7707 versus 0.7963)
while its KL divergence is about 34 × 34\times larger. The co-evolution
branch receives strictly more information than Condition A, including paired
comparisons and repair targets, yet because all
objectives update the same shared adapter, auxiliary learning interferes with
the generation policy. Training pass rate should therefore be treated as a
diagnostic, not a final quality metric. These pass@ k k magnitudes are
single-seed trends rather than significance claims; the KL and length-collapse
diagnostics, which are large and monotonic, are the more robust signal.
blocks.zh:
SPARK风格的共演化适用于代码生成,但它在跨基准HumanEval上并不比执行时只执行的GPRO. 在比对处
重复 5, C-reg2 线索 人类Eval 通道上的 A- long@ 1 (0.7707对0.7963)
而它的KL差值大约是34×34\时。 共同进化
分支接收的信息严格地多于条件A,包括配对
比较和修复目标,然而,因为
目标更新相同的共享适配器,辅助学习干扰
生成政策。 因此,应将培训合格率视为
诊断,而不是最后的质量衡量标准。 这些通过@ kk 星等为
单一种子趋势而不是意义索赔;KL和长度缩合
诊断器是大型的和单调的,是较强的信号。

blocks.en:
Single-adapter co-evolution may be too architecturally entangled for the code
setting. Code generation breaks the structural symmetry SPARK relies on in
reasoning tasks: in math and visual reasoning, rollout, judgment, and
reflection outputs all resemble a reasoning trace followed by an answer,
whereas in code, policy rollouts are full programs, pairwise targets are single
tokens, and reflection targets are full code conditioned on a different prompt.
Training one shared adapter on this heterogeneous mixture is a harder
distribution-balancing problem, and the observed length collapse is consistent
with that mismatch.

blocks.en:
A caveat applies to how strongly this speaks to co-evolution in general. Our
auxiliary mixture is reflection-dominated, and reflection uses canonical or
correct-rollout targets rather than verified self-fix trajectories. The length
collapse and below-baseline reflection fix rate are therefore partially
entangled: we cannot fully separate heterogeneous-target drift from weak
reflection construction. The failure we document is for a reflection-heavy,
canonical-target mixture co-updating a single adapter, not for all co-evolution
weightings. Our result aligns with SCoRe’s distribution-shift and
behavior-collapse predictions [ 10 ] , and with the pattern reported
concurrently by Choi et al. [ 17 ] in code-repair self-play,
where generator-fixer training improves repair on self-generated bugs while
degrading repair on human-authored bugs.

blocks.en:
Several prior approaches give code-generation models a reasoning or explanation
channel without SPARK-style co-evolution. Chain-of-thought, Self-Debug, and
Reflexion use prompting, execution feedback, or verbal reflection at inference
time or in separate training formats [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . Concurrent
code self-improvement methods factor the policy and auxiliary roles
differently. ACE [ 21 ] trains the model both to solve problems and to generate
adversarial unit tests that expose flaws in its own solutions, while GASP
(Guided Asymmetric Self-Play) uses a teacher-student setup in which one role
poses problems and the other solves them [ 22 ] . Both report improved code-generation performance from self-improvement, which is consistent with our interpretation that the
limitation lies not in self-improvement on code in general, but in the design
choices studied here, particularly co-updating a single shared adapter with
heterogeneous objectives.

blocks.en:
Within co-evolution, separating the policy adapter from a dedicated auxiliary
adapter on a shared base model is the most promising direction we see, and we
are not aware of prior work testing it for code generation. Methods that avoid
co-evolution entirely, such as preference optimization from execution-labeled
pairs, are a separate direction. Better reflection
may also require verified repair trajectories and reference-anchored fixer
training [ 17 ] , together with held-out monitoring to avoid
proxy-reward over-optimization [ 16 ] . More broadly, even when
feedback comes from executable unit tests rather than a learned reward model,
co-evolving generation and evaluation within one adapter can produce training
gains that do not transfer. Stronger supervision alone may therefore not be sufficient; architectural separation between generator and evaluator may also be needed.
blocks.zh:
在共同演变中,将政策调整器与专用辅助设备分开

不清楚是否在代码生成中进行了前期工作测试。 避免的方法

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
This study evaluates a single model at a single scale using a single random
seed over six iterations, so the pass@ k k differences we report are trends
rather than significant effects. HumanEval is also a widely used benchmark, so
we cannot rule out that some of its problems appeared in the pretraining data
of the model we fine-tune.

我们无法排除某些问题出现在预训数据中

blocks.en:
Because the co-evolution condition adds an auxiliary update phase, it takes
more optimizer steps than the baseline. We did not run a step-matched
comparison, in which the baseline receives the same number of updates, so we
cannot separate the effect of additional training from that of the auxiliary
objectives. We also do not compare against ACE [ 21 ] or
GASP [ 22 ] , which factor the policy and auxiliary roles differently.
Finally, our auxiliary mixture is dominated by reflection, whose weight is
twenty times that of pairwise comparison. The results therefore do not speak to
co-evolution under other weightings.
